AP® World History Unit 1: Belief systems, c. 1200–1450

6 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

Aligned to AP World History: Modern, Unit 1 · 1.1 Developments in East Asia from c. 1200 to c. 1450; Unit 1 · 1.2 Developments in Dar al-Islam from c. 1200 to c. 1450; Unit 1 · 1.3 Developments in South and Southeast Asia from c. 1200 to c. 1450

Short, curiosity-driven missions (about 20 minutes each) that teachers can assign. Use them alongside AP Classroom practice.

  1. Mission 1How did scattered Jewish communities keep one faith under rulers who welcomed or expelled them?
  2. Mission 2How did faith in a crucified teacher come to shape popes, monks and an African kingdom?

Mission 1

Mission 1: How did scattered Jewish communities keep one faith under rulers who welcomed or expelled them?

Make a guess: How did scattered Jewish communities keep one faith under rulers who welcomed or expelled them?

Mission 1

One God and the covenant

  • Judaism is monotheistic: one God, creator of everything.
  • "HEAR, O ISRAEL: THE LORD OUR GOD, THE LORD IS ONE." (Deuteronomy 6:4, JPS 1917) This is the Shema, said daily.
  • Jews believe in a covenant (brit): a binding agreement between God and the Jewish people.
  • With Abraham: "to be a God unto thee and to thy seed after thee" (Genesis 17:7, JPS 1917).
  • Jews believe that at Sinai God gave the Torah through Moses, and the people promised to keep its commandments.
  • Many Jews understand being chosen as a responsibility: to live by God's law, not a claim to be better than others.
Mission 1

Torah, Tanakh, Talmud

  • Torah: the five books of Moses (Genesis to Deuteronomy); traditionally 613 commandments (mitzvot).
  • Tanakh (the Hebrew Bible): Torah (teaching) + Nevi'im (prophets) + Ketuvim (writings).
  • Christians call these books the Old Testament; Jews do not.
  • Oral Torah: teaching passed on alongside the written text, later written in the Mishnah (c. 200 CE).
  • Talmud: the Mishnah plus centuries of rabbis' debate on it; the Babylonian Talmud was completed c. 500–600 CE.
  • The Talmud became the core of Jewish study and law wherever Jews lived.
Mission 1

Synagogue, rabbis, Shabbat, kashrut

  • After the Romans destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem (70 CE), worship centered on the synagogue: a house of prayer, study and meeting.
  • Rabbis: teachers and interpreters of Jewish law (halakha), not priests.
  • Shabbat: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." (Exodus 20:8, JPS 1917) From Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall: rest, prayer, family meals.
  • Kashrut: food laws (e.g. no pork or shellfish, meat and milk kept apart); food that follows them is kosher.
  • These practices could be kept anywhere, with no temple and no Jewish state.
Quick check
?After 70 CE, what allowed Jewish communities in Baghdad, Cairo and Mainz to keep the same faith?
Mission 1

Diaspora communities

  • Diaspora: Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel.
  • Sephardi Jews: from the Iberian Peninsula (Sefarad = Spain); later spoke Judeo-Spanish (Ladino).
  • Ashkenazi Jews: from the Rhineland, then Central and Eastern Europe; spoke Yiddish.
  • Mizrahi and other communities lived across the Middle East, North Africa, Yemen, Persia, India and Ethiopia.
  • All shared Torah and Talmud; customs, melodies and some legal rulings differed.
Mission 1

Under Muslim rule

  • In Dar al-Islam, Jews and Christians were dhimmi: "protected people" of scripture.
  • They could worship and run their own courts, but paid a special tax (jizya) and faced limits (e.g. on building, dress, office).
  • Treatment varied by ruler and period, from good to harsh.
  • Many Jews worked as merchants, doctors and scholars, in Arabic.
  • Moses Maimonides (1138–1204): born in Córdoba, worked as a physician in Cairo; wrote a great code of Jewish law (the Mishneh Torah, in Hebrew) and philosophy (the Guide for the Perplexed, in Arabic).
  • The Cairo Geniza (a synagogue storeroom) preserves letters of Jewish traders across the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean.
Mission 1

In Christian Europe

  • Jews were often a protected but restricted minority, dependent on kings and bishops.
  • Barred from many guilds and from owning land in many places; some turned to trade and moneylending, which Church law limited for Christians.
  • Violence: Crusaders massacred Rhineland Jews (1096); false charges such as blood libel led to attacks.
  • Expulsions: England (1290), France (1306, again 1394), many German towns.
  • Ghettos: Venice (1516) required Jews to live in one walled quarter.
  • Yet Jewish learning flourished, e.g. Rashi (1040–1105) of France, whose commentaries are still studied.
Quick check
?Which comparison of Jewish life c. 1200–1450 is most accurate?
Mission 1

1492: expulsion from Spain and Portugal

  • 1478: the Spanish Inquisition began investigating conversos (Jews who had converted to Christianity, many under pressure).
  • 1492: after conquering Granada, Ferdinand and Isabella ordered all Jews to convert or leave (the Alhambra Decree).
  • Tens of thousands left; many others converted.
  • 1496–97: Portugal ordered Jews out too, then forced most to convert rather than let them go.
  • Stated aim: religious unity in the newly joined Catholic kingdoms of Castile and Aragon (historians debate other motives; see the later screen).
Mission 1

Welcome in the Ottoman Empire

  • Sultan Bayezid II (r. 1481–1512) allowed Sephardi refugees to settle.
  • Major communities grew in Istanbul and Salonica (Thessaloniki), and later Safed in Galilee.
  • Refugees brought skills in trade, medicine and printing.
  • As dhimmi, they kept their own law and leaders, paid the jizya and lived under limits.
  • Other refuges: North Africa, Italy, and later Amsterdam.
Mission 1Evaluate

Why accommodate or expel?

  • Claim to weigh: "Religion was the main reason rulers expelled or welcomed Jews."
  • Reasons for: Spain sought a single Catholic faith; Ottoman law gave protected status to "people of the book".
  • Reasons against: money and skills mattered: rulers seized Jewish property or gained skilled subjects; politics mattered: winning popularity or building a strong state.
  • Judge it by: What did each ruler gain? Did policy change when needs changed? Which sources show motives, not just actions?
Quick check
?Which statement best explains why the Ottoman Empire accepted Jewish refugees after 1492?
Mission check

?In 1264, Duke Bolesław of Greater Poland granted a charter protecting Jews' lives, property, trade and synagogues, as Jewish merchants moved east from German lands. Which pattern does this case best fit?

Jewish faith traveled in texts, laws and homes; how a community fared depended on each ruler's goals.

Mission 2

Mission 2: How did faith in a crucified teacher come to shape popes, monks and an African kingdom?

Make a guess: How did faith in a crucified teacher come to shape popes, monks and an African kingdom?

Mission 2

Jesus

  • Jesus of Nazareth (c. 4 BCE–c. 30 CE): a Jewish teacher in Roman-ruled Judea.
  • Taught about the kingdom of God, love of God and neighbor, forgiveness; known for healings and parables.
  • Crucified by the Roman authorities in Jerusalem.
  • His followers proclaimed he had risen from the dead and was the Messiah (Greek: Christos, "anointed one").
  • Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God.
Mission 2

Trinity and incarnation

  • Christians are monotheists: one God.
  • Trinity: one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, equal and eternal.
  • Defined in the Nicene Creed (325, expanded 381).
  • Incarnation: God the Son became fully human in Jesus, while remaining fully God.
  • "The Word became flesh and lived amongst us." (John 1:14, WEBBE)
Mission 2Read the source

Death, resurrection, salvation

Translation: World English Bible, British Edition (WEBBE).

  • "Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, … he was buried, … he was raised on the third day" (1 Corinthians 15:3–4)
  • "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life." (John 3:16)
  • Salvation: being saved from sin and its result (separation from God) and brought to eternal life.

Q1 What two events does Paul put at the heart of the faith?

Show answer

Christ's death for sins and his resurrection.

Q2 According to John 3:16, what does God's love lead to for believers?

Show answer

Eternal life.

Mission 2

Bible and sacraments

  • Bible: the Old Testament (the Hebrew scriptures, shared with Judaism) + the New Testament (Gospels, Acts, letters, Revelation).
  • Sacraments: rituals that Christians believe give God's grace.
  • In medieval Catholic and Orthodox churches: seven, including baptism (entry into the Church) and the Eucharist (bread and wine, Christ's body and blood; also called Mass or Holy Communion).
  • The others: confirmation, confession (penance), marriage, ordination, anointing of the sick.
  • Sacraments marked a person's life from birth to death, so the Church was present at every stage.
Quick check
?A student says: "The incarnation is the belief that Jesus rose from the dead on the third day." What is the error?
Mission 2

East and West split (1054)

  • After Rome's fall in the west, two centers grew apart: Rome (Latin) and Constantinople (Greek, the Byzantine Empire).
  • Disputes: the pope's authority over all Christians; a phrase added in the West to the creed (the Spirit proceeds from the Father "and the Son", filioque); bread used in the Eucharist.
  • 1054: the pope's envoy and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other.
  • Result: the Roman Catholic Church (led by the pope) and the Eastern Orthodox Church (self-governing churches led by patriarchs; icons central to worship).
  • The split hardened after crusaders sacked Constantinople (1204).
Mission 2

The Church in medieval Europe

  • Papacy: popes claimed spiritual authority over kings; conflicts such as the Investiture Controversy (over who appoints bishops, 1075–1122).
  • Monasteries: monks and nuns living under a rule (e.g. the Rule of St Benedict, 6th century): prayer, work, copying books, schools, hospitals, farming.
  • Parish churches: sacraments, tithes (a tenth of produce), the Church calendar and feast days.
  • Pilgrimage: journeys to holy places (Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela, Canterbury) for prayer and penance.
  • Crusades (from 1095): wars called by popes to take Jerusalem.
  • The Church was Europe's largest landowner and main center of learning.
Quick check
?Which was a major role of monasteries in medieval Europe?
Mission 2

Christian Ethiopia

  • Aksum: King Ezana adopted Christianity in the 4th century, among the earliest states to do so.
  • The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is linked to the Coptic Church of Alexandria; its bishops came from Egypt for centuries; worship in the Ge'ez language.
  • Lalibela (late 12th–early 13th century): churches carved from solid rock, planned as a "new Jerusalem" when pilgrimage to Jerusalem was hard.
  • Solomonic dynasty (from 1270): kings claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, a story told in the Kebra Nagast; faith and kingship were tied together.
  • Contrast: in the Hausa city-states of West Africa, rulers of Kano and Katsina adopted Islam (14th–15th centuries), which linked them to Muslim trade networks.
Mission 2

Christians in Asia

  • The Church of the East spread from Persia along the Silk Roads to Central Asia and China.
  • A stone monument at Xi'an (781) records Christian monks in Tang China.
  • Some Mongol leaders' families were Christian; Church of the East bishops served across Asia.
  • St Thomas Christians in Kerala, India, trace their church to the apostle Thomas.
  • In Asia, Christians were usually minorities under Muslim, Buddhist or other rulers.
Quick check
?What made Christianity in Ethiopia distinctive compared with Christianity in medieval Western Europe?
Mission check

?In 988, Prince Vladimir of Kyiv was baptized and invited clergy from Constantinople to teach his people. After 1054, which church would Rus' Christians belong to, and what would their worship feature?

Shared beliefs and sacraments shaped every church, but each society shaped its church in turn: Roman, Byzantine, Ethiopian or Asian.

Mission 3

Mission 3: How did Islam spread across three continents, and why did a question about leadership divide empires?

Make a guess: How did Islam spread across three continents, and why did a question about leadership divide empires?

Mission 3

The Prophet and the Qur'an

  • Muhammad (c. 570–632) lived in Mecca, Arabia.
  • Muslims believe that from 610 God (Allah, Arabic for "God") revealed the Qur'an to him through the angel Jibril (Gabriel).
  • 622: the Hijra, his move to Medina, where the first Muslim community formed; year 1 of the Islamic calendar.
  • Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's own word, in Arabic; Muslim tradition holds it was gathered into one standard text soon after his death.
  • Muslims honor earlier prophets, including Ibrahim (Abraham), Musa (Moses) and Isa (Jesus); Muhammad is the last.
Mission 3Read the source

One God, the last prophet

Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930).

  • "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him." (Qur'an 112:1–4)
  • "Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but he is the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets" (Qur'an 33:40)
  • Tawhid: the absolute oneness of God, the heart of Islam.

Q1 Which line of Surah 112 do Muslims read as ruling out the idea that God has a Son?

Show answer

"He begetteth not nor was begotten."

Q2 What does "Seal of the Prophets" mean for Muslims?

Show answer

Muhammad is the final prophet; no prophet comes after him.

Mission 3

The Five Pillars

  • Shahada: declaration of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.
  • Salat: prayer five times a day, facing the Kaaba in Mecca.
  • Zakat: giving a set share of wealth (usually 2.5% of savings a year) to those in need.
  • Sawm: fasting from dawn to sunset in the month of Ramadan.
  • Hajj: pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime for those able.
  • Shared practice united Muslims across very different societies.
Mission 3

Sunna, sharia, ummah

  • Sunna: the Prophet's example (words and actions), recorded in reports called hadith.
  • Sharia: God's law or "path" for all of life: worship, family, trade, crime.
  • Scholars (ulama) interpret it through fiqh (jurisprudence); Sunni Muslims follow several schools of law, Shi'a Muslims their own (Ja'fari).
  • Ummah: the worldwide community of Muslims, beyond tribe or nation.
  • Qadis (judges) applied sharia, so scholars and courts gave Muslim societies a shared legal culture.
Quick check
?A merchant from Mali on Hajj in Mecca prays beside pilgrims from Persia and India. What best explains how they share the same practices?
Mission 3Diversity

Sunni and Shi'a

  • 632: the Prophet died. Who should lead the community?
  • Sunni view: leading companions chose Abu Bakr as the first caliph ("successor"); the first four caliphs are honored as rightly guided.
  • Shi'a view: the Prophet had named his cousin and son-in-law Ali; leadership belongs to Ali and his descendants, the Imams.
  • 680: Ali's son Husayn was killed at Karbala; Shi'a Muslims mourn him each year at Ashura.
  • Both share the Qur'an, tawhid, the Prophet and the core practices; they differ on leadership, some law and some rituals.
  • Sunni Muslims are the large majority worldwide; Shi'a are the majority in Iran.
Mission 3

Caliphates and Turkic states

  • Umayyad caliphs (661–750) ruled from Damascus; Abbasid caliphs (750–1258) from Baghdad.
  • From the 900s the Abbasid realm fragmented: local dynasties ruled while the caliph kept religious prestige.
  • Seljuk Turks took Baghdad (1055) and ruled as sultans ("holders of power").
  • Mamluk Sultanate (1250–1517), Egypt: rulers from slave-soldier origins; beat the Mongols (1260).
  • Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526): Turkic and Afghan dynasties ruled much of north India.
  • 1258: Mongols sacked Baghdad and ended the Abbasid caliphate there.
Mission 3

How Islam spread

  • Conquest (7th–8th centuries): Arab armies took Persia, Syria, Egypt, North Africa and Spain (711).
  • Conversion under Muslim rule was mostly gradual, over centuries; Muslims cite "There is no compulsion in religion." (Qur'an 2:256)
  • Merchants: across the Indian Ocean (East African coast, India, Southeast Asia) and the Sahara (Mali, where Mansa Musa made his famous Hajj in 1324).
  • Sufis: mystics seeking direct closeness to God through prayer, music and remembrance (dhikr); their orders and shrines drew converts, e.g. the Chishti order in India.
  • Some Muslims, then and now, criticize certain Sufi practices.
Quick check
?Which statement best describes how Islam spread in Southeast Asia, c. 1200–1450?
Mission 3

House of Wisdom and beyond

  • House of Wisdom in Abbasid Baghdad (flourished under Caliph al-Ma'mun, r. 813–833): scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic.
  • They preserved and commented on Greek philosophy and science (Aristotle, Galen, Ptolemy).
  • al-Khwarizmi (9th century): algebra; the word "algorithm" comes from his name.
  • Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (1201–1274): mathematician and astronomer; built the Maragha observatory (1259) under Mongol rule.
  • Ibn Sina (980–1037): the Canon of Medicine, later used in European universities.
  • Via Spain and Sicily, these works passed into Latin Europe.
Mission 3

Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal rivalry

  • Ottoman Empire (Sunni): after conquering Mamluk Egypt (1517), its sultans also claimed the title of caliph.
  • Safavid Empire, Persia: Shah Ismail I (1501) made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion, bringing Shi'a scholars to teach it.
  • Battle of Chaldiran (1514): the Ottomans defeated the Safavids; a first peace came at Amasya (1555), but wars went on, off and on, until 1639.
  • Each side cast the other as religiously wrong, which hardened the Sunni–Shi'a split.
  • Mughal Empire (Sunni rulers in India) fought the Safavids over the border city of Kandahar, mainly for territory and trade.
  • Religion mixed with power: rivals used religious identity to rally support.
Quick check
?Why did Ottoman–Safavid rivalry deepen the divide between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims?
Mission 3

Faith and resistance to empire

  • Sokoto Caliphate (founded 1809, today's Nigeria): the scholar Usman dan Fodio led a jihad against Hausa rulers he judged unjust and lax in Islam.
  • Mahdist war, Sudan: Muhammad Ahmad declared himself the Mahdi (a guide expected before the end of time) in 1881; his forces took Khartoum (1885) from Egyptian-British control; British troops defeated them in 1898.
  • All-India Muslim League (founded 1906): argued that Muslims in British India needed political protection; under Muhammad Ali Jinnah it led the demand for Pakistan (1947).
  • Religious identity could unite people against outside or unjust rule.
Mission check

?In 18th-century Lucknow, India, the ruling nawabs paid for grand processions each year to mourn the death of Husayn at Karbala. Which branch of Islam did these rulers most likely follow?

Shared beliefs made one ummah from Spain to Indonesia; a question about leadership grew into rival branches, and rival empires used it.

Mission 4

Mission 4: How did Hindu ideas about the soul, duty and devotion shape lives and kingdoms from India to Cambodia?

Make a guess: How did Hindu ideas about the soul, duty and devotion shape lives and kingdoms from India to Cambodia?

Mission 4

Brahman and atman

  • Hinduism is a family of traditions from South Asia, with no single founder or creed.
  • Many Hindus speak of Brahman: the one ultimate reality behind everything that exists.
  • Each living being has an atman: a true, eternal self (soul).
  • How are they related? Hindu schools give different answers:
  • Advaita (Shankara, c. 8th century): atman and Brahman are one. Sanskrit: tat tvam asi, "you are that" (Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7).
  • Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja, c. 1017–1137) and Dvaita (Madhva, 13th century): the self depends on God, or is distinct from God, and is joined to God by devotion.
Mission 4

Dharma, karma, samsara, moksha

  • Dharma: duty and right order; what is right for you to do, given your stage of life and place in society.
  • Karma: action and its results. Good and bad actions shape future experience.
  • Samsara: the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. The atman is reborn in new bodies.
  • Moksha: liberation from samsara, the highest goal.
  • Link: follow your dharma → good karma → better rebirth; moksha ends the cycle.
  • Three classic paths (margas) toward moksha: knowledge (jnana), selfless action (karma), devotion (bhakti).
Quick check
?A student writes: "Karma means your whole life is fixed in advance, so nothing you do now can change it." Why would most Hindus disagree?
Mission 4Diversity

Many deities, three great streams

  • Many Hindus see the many deities as forms or faces of the one divine reality.
  • Vaishnava: devotion to Vishnu, preserver of the world, and his avatars (descents) such as Rama and Krishna.
  • Shaiva: devotion to Shiva as the supreme God, often linked with destruction and renewal; often worshiped through the linga symbol.
  • Shakta: devotion to the Goddess (Devi, Shakti): divine power as female, in forms such as Durga and Kali.
  • Smarta Hindus worship several deities side by side.
  • These streams overlap: one family may visit both Vishnu and Shiva temples.
Mission 4

The sacred texts

  • Vedas: the oldest hymns and rituals, in Sanskrit; the Rig Veda goes back to roughly 1500–1200 BCE (many scholars' estimate).
  • Upanishads: later Vedic texts that explore Brahman and atman (the oldest c. 800–500 BCE).
  • These are shruti, "what is heard": revealed truth.
  • Smriti, "what is remembered": the epics Ramayana and Mahabharata, law books, and later Puranas (stories of the deities).
  • The Bhagavad Gita ("Song of the Lord") is part of the Mahabharata: Krishna teaches the warrior prince Arjuna on a battlefield.
Mission 4Read the source

The Bhagavad Gita

Translation: Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885).

  • On the soul: "as when one layeth / His worn-out robes away, / And taking new ones…" so the spirit puts off the body and takes a new one (Bhagavad Gita 2:22, Arnold, partly paraphrase).
  • On duty: "Let right deeds be / Thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them." (Bhagavad Gita 2:47, Arnold)
  • On devotion: "Whoso shall offer Me in faith and love / A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water poured forth, / That offering I accept" (Bhagavad Gita 9:26, Arnold)

Q1 Which belief does the image of changing robes illustrate?

Show answer

Samsara: the eternal atman takes a new body at rebirth.

Q2 What does 9:26 suggest about who can worship?

Show answer

Anyone: a simple gift offered with love is accepted. This idea fed the bhakti movement.

Mission 4

Varna and jati

  • Varna: an ideal scheme of four social classes found in Vedic and law texts: Brahmins (priests, teachers), Kshatriyas (rulers, warriors), Vaishyas (merchants, farmers), Shudras (laborers, servants).
  • Jati: the thousands of local birth groups people actually lived in, often tied to an occupation; people usually married within their jati.
  • Groups treated as outside the varnas faced exclusion as "untouchable"; today many call themselves Dalits.
  • Hierarchy varied by region and changed over time; groups could rise in status.
  • Hindus have long debated it: many bhakti saints rejected caste pride; India's constitution (1950) abolished untouchability.
  • Europeans later called the whole system caste (from Portuguese casta).
Quick check
?Which statement about varna and jati is most accurate for the period c. 1200–1450?
Mission 4

The bhakti movement

  • Bhakti: loving devotion to a personal god.
  • Began with Tamil poet-saints in South India (c. 6th–9th centuries): the Alvars (devotees of Vishnu) and Nayanars (devotees of Shiva).
  • Spread north over centuries; poets sang in local languages, not only Sanskrit.
  • Famous voices: Mirabai (16th century), a Rajput princess devoted to Krishna; Kabir (15th century), a weaver who drew on Hindu and Muslim ideas; Ravidas, a leatherworker poet.
  • Message: God can be reached by anyone through love, whatever their caste or sex, without needing priests.
  • It grew alongside Islamic Sufism, which also stressed love of God (see the Islam mission).
Mission 4

Kings, temples and dharma

  • A Hindu king was expected to protect dharma: keep order, defend his people, support Brahmins and temples.
  • Great temples were centers of worship, landholding, trade, art and festivals; building one showed a king's piety and power.
  • Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646), South India: capital at Hampi with huge temples; a rival of the Deccan sultanates; its capital was sacked after the Battle of Talikota (1565).
  • Rajput kingdoms, northwest India: warrior clans claiming Kshatriya status; fought the Delhi Sultanate, later many allied with the Mughals.
  • Khmer Empire (c. 802–1431), Cambodia: Angkor Wat (early 1100s, King Suryavarman II) was built for Vishnu; later kings were Buddhist.
  • Majapahit (1293–c. 1527), Java: a Hindu-Buddhist sea empire.
Quick check
?Why did Khmer kings build temples such as Angkor Wat in a region far from India?
Mission 4

Ahimsa and Gandhi

  • Ahimsa: non-harming, an ancient ideal shared by Hindus, Jains and Buddhists.
  • Mohandas Gandhi (1869–1948) read the Bhagavad Gita as a guide to selfless action and drew on ahimsa (and on Jain, Christian and other ideas).
  • He called his method satyagraha ("holding firmly to truth"): nonviolent resistance to injustice.
  • Used against British rule in India, e.g. the Salt March (1930).
  • Some Hindus disagreed with him, and his assassin (1948) was a Hindu nationalist.
  • Martin Luther King Jr. later drew on Gandhi's methods (more in the religion and political power missions).
Mission 4Worked answer

Belief → evidence → effect

Question: Explain one way Hindu beliefs shaped states in South or Southeast Asia, c. 1200–1450.

  • Belief: A king's duty (dharma) was to protect the sacred order and support worship.
  • Evidence: Vijayanagara rulers built and endowed great temples at Hampi.
  • Effect: Temple building made the rulers look legitimate and tied priests, merchants and farmers to the state.
  • AP short-answer tip: name a specific state or example, then explain how the belief caused the effect.
Mission check

?A 16th-century poet from a royal family refuses the rituals her in-laws expect, sings in a local language about her love for Krishna, and welcomes listeners of any caste. Which belief best explains her choices?

Hindu beliefs worked at every level: the soul's journey, a person's duty, a poet's devotion and a king's temple.

Mission 5

Mission 5: How did one teacher's answer to suffering spread from India to Japan, Tibet and Java?

Make a guess: How did one teacher's answer to suffering spread from India to Japan, Tibet and Java?

Mission 5

The Buddha's question

  • Siddhartha Gautama, a prince in northern South Asia (c. 5th century BCE).
  • Tradition: he saw old age, sickness, death and a holy wanderer, and left home to understand suffering.
  • Tradition continues: after years of extreme fasting, he chose a Middle Way between luxury and harsh self-denial.
  • Buddhists believe that, meditating at Bodh Gaya, he gained enlightenment and became the Buddha, "the awakened one".
  • He kept the ideas of samsara (rebirth) and karma from his setting, but taught a new way out.
  • First sermon: the Deer Park at Sarnath.
Mission 5Read the source

The Three Marks

Translation: F. Max Müller, The Dhammapada (1881).

  • "All created things perish" (Dhammapada 277) → anicca: impermanence.
  • "All created things are grief and pain" (Dhammapada 278) → dukkha: suffering, unsatisfactoriness.
  • "All forms are unreal" (Dhammapada 279) → anatta: no fixed, permanent self.

Q1 Which mark most clearly separates Buddhism from the Hindu idea of atman?

Show answer

Anatta: there is no eternal, unchanging self.

Q2 Why would impermanence lead to suffering?

Show answer

People cling to things that cannot last.

Mission 5

The Four Noble Truths

  • 1. Dukkha: life involves suffering and dissatisfaction.
  • 2. Samudaya: suffering has a cause: craving (tanha) and attachment.
  • 3. Nirodha: suffering can end, when craving ends.
  • 4. Magga: the way to end it is the Eightfold Path.
  • Often compared to a doctor: diagnosis → cause → cure is possible → treatment.
Mission 5

The Eightfold Path

  • Not eight steps in order, but eight parts practiced together (the wheel has eight spokes).
  • Wisdom: right view, right intention.
  • Ethics: right speech, right action, right livelihood.
  • Meditation: right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.
  • Lay Buddhists keep the Five Precepts: no killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying or intoxicants.
Quick check
?According to the Four Noble Truths, what is the main cause of suffering?
Mission 5

Nirvana

  • Nirvana (Pali: nibbana) means "blowing out", like a flame.
  • What is blown out: the "three fires" of greed, hatred and delusion.
  • Result: an end to craving, an end to suffering, and no more rebirth.
  • It is not a heaven or a place, and not simple nothingness; Buddhists say words cannot fully describe it.
  • "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." (Dhammapada 5, Müller)
Mission 5

The sangha and monasticism

  • Three Jewels (refuges): the Buddha, the Dharma (teaching), the Sangha (community).
  • The sangha includes monks (bhikkhus) and nuns (bhikkhunis) who follow a code of discipline (Vinaya).
  • Laypeople give food and gifts (dana) and gain merit; monks teach and give an example.
  • Monasteries became centers of learning, copying texts and teaching: e.g. Nalanda in India (from c. 5th century CE).
  • Monasteries attracted gifts of land from kings, linking the sangha to royal power.
Quick check
?Why did many Asian rulers give land and wealth to Buddhist monasteries?
Mission 5Diversity

Three branches

  • Theravada ("teaching of the elders"): Pali scriptures; ideal of the arhat, who reaches nirvana through their own practice; strong monastic sangha. Sri Lanka, Burma (Myanmar), Thailand, Laos, Cambodia.
  • Mahayana ("great vehicle"): ideal of the bodhisattva, who vows to help all beings reach enlightenment out of compassion; many buddhas and bodhisattvas revered; schools such as Pure Land and Chan (Zen). China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam.
  • Tibetan (Vajrayana, "diamond vehicle"): builds on Mahayana with ritual, chanting (mantras) and teachers called lamas; the Dalai Lama line from the 1500s. Tibet, Mongolia, Bhutan.
  • All share the Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths and the goal of awakening.
Mission 5

How Buddhism spread

  • Ashoka (Mauryan emperor, r. c. 268–232 BCE) supported Buddhism and sent missions, including to Sri Lanka.
  • Silk Roads: monks and merchants carried Buddhism to Central Asia and China (by the 1st century CE), then Korea (4th century) and Japan (6th century).
  • Chinese pilgrims such as Xuanzang (602–664) traveled to India and brought texts home.
  • Sea routes of the Indian Ocean carried it to Southeast Asia.
  • Buddhism adapted to each place; in India itself it declined by about the 13th century.
Mission 5

Buddhist states

  • Srivijaya (c. 7th–13th centuries), Sumatra: a sea-trade empire controlling the Strait of Malacca; a center of Mahayana learning where Chinese monks studied.
  • Nearby in Java, the Sailendra dynasty built Borobudur (c. 800), a vast Mahayana monument.
  • Sukhothai kingdom (c. 1238–1438), Thailand: kings such as Ram Khamhaeng supported Theravada monks from Sri Lanka.
  • Sinhala dynasties, Sri Lanka: kings protected the sangha and the Tooth Relic of the Buddha; their chronicles tie kingship to Buddhism.
  • Pattern: kings gained legitimacy as protectors of the Dharma; monasteries gained land and royal support.
Quick check
?A traveler in 13th-century Thailand meets monks who aim to become arhats and study Pali texts brought from Sri Lanka. Which branch is this?
Mission check

?In 9th-century Japan, a monk teaches that everyone should vow to keep working, life after life, until all beings are freed from suffering. Which idea is he teaching?

One teaching, many forms: Buddhism traveled with monks and merchants and took a different shape in each society.

Mission 6

Mission 6: Why did China choose its officials by testing them on ancient books about family and good conduct?

Make a guess: Why did China choose its officials by testing them on ancient books about family and good conduct?

Mission 6

Confucius and the Analects

  • Confucius (Kongzi, traditionally 551–479 BCE) lived in an age of war between rival states.
  • His question: how can families and states live in harmony?
  • His answer: rulers and people must become good, through study, self-discipline and right relationships.
  • His sayings were collected by followers in the Analects (Lunyu).
  • Confucianism is often called a philosophy, a tradition or a religion: it includes rituals for ancestors and Heaven (Tian), but has no priesthood or single creed.
Mission 6

Ren, li, xiao

  • Ren: humaneness, goodness toward others; the highest virtue.
  • Li (ritual): proper conduct, ceremony and manners that train people in respect.
  • Xiao: filial piety: respect, care and obedience toward parents and ancestors, during life and after death.
  • Junzi: the "exemplary person" who lives these virtues; the model for officials.
  • Rule by virtue and example, not mainly by punishment.
Mission 6

Five relationships and gender

  • Five key relationships (listed by the later thinker Mencius, 4th century BCE): ruler–subject, father–son, husband–wife, elder–younger brother, friend–friend.
  • Four of the five are unequal: the senior gives care and guidance; the junior gives loyalty and respect.
  • Women: honored as mothers (filial piety applies to mothers too) and expected to manage the household.
  • But also expected to defer: the "three obediences" to father, then husband, then son.
  • The female scholar Ban Zhao (c. 45–c. 117 CE) wrote Lessons for Women, urging humility and also education for girls.
  • In the Song era, ideals of widow chastity grew stricter, and foot-binding spread among elite families.
Quick check
?Which statement best describes Confucian expectations of women in Song China?
Mission 6

Exams and the Song state

  • Song dynasty (960–1279) relied on a large bureaucracy of scholar-officials.
  • Officials were chosen through civil service examinations on the Confucian classics (begun under the Sui, expanded under the Song).
  • Logic: a man who mastered the classics had the moral training to govern well.
  • Printing made books cheaper, so more men could study.
  • In theory open to talent; in practice, years of study favored wealthy families.
  • The system bound the elite to the state and justified imperial rule as rule by virtue (with the older idea of the Mandate of Heaven).
Mission 6Read the source

The Analects

The Analects (paraphrase; chapter numbers as in James Legge's 1861 translation):

  • If people are led by virtue and ritual, they will feel shame at wrongdoing and become good; laws and punishments alone only make them avoid getting caught (Analects 2:3, paraphrase).
  • Feeding your parents is not enough: even animals are fed. Without reverence, what is the difference? (Analects 2:7, paraphrase)
  • Asked for one word to guide a whole life, Confucius answered "reciprocity": do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself (Analects 15:23, paraphrase).

Q1 According to 2:3, why should rulers govern by virtue?

Show answer

It changes people's hearts, not just their behavior.

Q2 What does 2:7 add to the idea of filial piety?

Show answer

Respect and attitude matter, not only material care.

Mission 6

Daoism (background)

  • Beyond the AP framework, for World Religions courses.
  • The Dao ("the Way"): the source and flow of all things, beyond words.
  • The Daodejing is credited to Laozi (traditionally 6th century BCE; many scholars doubt he was a single historical person); the Zhuangzi is another key text.
  • Wu wei: "non-forcing" action: act naturally, like water, without struggle.
  • Ideals: simplicity, harmony with nature, balance of yin and yang.
  • Later religious Daoism developed temples, priests, rituals and practices for long life.
Mission 6

Confucian and Daoist contrasts

  • Beyond the AP framework, for World Religions courses.
  • Confucian focus: society, ritual, study, duty, active government.
  • Daoist focus: nature, spontaneity, simplicity, less government.
  • Many Chinese drew on both, and on Buddhism: the saying "three teachings" names this mix.
  • A common saying: an official was Confucian at work and Daoist in retirement.
Mission 6

Buddhism in China

  • Buddhism reached China by the 1st century CE along the Silk Roads (see the Buddhism mission).
  • Mahayana schools flourished: Chan (meditation; Zen in Japan) and Pure Land.
  • Critics said monks broke filial piety: they left their families and had no children to continue ancestor rites.
  • In 845 a Tang emperor closed thousands of monasteries.
  • Buddhism survived and stayed popular, but Confucian scholars wanted a fuller answer to its big questions.
Mission 6

Neo-Confucianism

  • Neo-Confucianism: a Song-era revival of Confucian thought.
  • Key thinker: Zhu Xi (1130–1200).
  • Borrowed big questions from Buddhism and Daoism: the nature of the universe, the mind, meditation ("quiet sitting").
  • Taught that all things have li (principle) (a different Chinese word from li, ritual) and qi (energy, matter).
  • Kept Confucian goals: family duty, public service, study; rejected withdrawal into monasteries.
  • Zhu Xi's commentaries on the Four Books became the standard for the exams (from 1313).
Quick check
?How did Neo-Confucianism respond to Buddhism and Daoism?
Mission 6

Spread across East Asia

  • Korea: Goryeo (918–1392) adopted exams (from 958) alongside Buddhism; the Joseon dynasty (1392–1897) made Neo-Confucianism its state ideology.
  • Heian Japan (794–1185): adopted Chinese characters, Buddhism, court ranks and Confucian ideals of loyalty; court women such as Murasaki Shikibu wrote in Japanese script; no lasting exam system.
  • Vietnam: the Ly dynasty built a Temple of Literature (1070) and held exams (from 1075) while staying independent of China.
  • Pattern: neighbors borrowed Chinese ideas and adapted them to their own rulers and traditions.
Mission check

?In 15th-century Korea, a young noble studies Zhu Xi's commentaries for the state exam and keeps strict mourning rites for his father. Which tradition is shaping his life most?

Confucian ideas turned family virtues into a way to run a state, and neighbors adopted them as a model.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Core beliefs: one God, the covenant, Torah, Tanakh and Talmud; practice in synagogue, home, Shabbat and kashrut kept communities together.
  • Jews lived as protected but restricted minorities under Muslim and Christian rule, with violence and expulsions at times.
  • 1492: expelled from Spain (Portugal 1496–97); many Sephardi Jews found refuge in the Ottoman Empire.

Mission 2

  • Core beliefs: Jesus as Son of God and Messiah; Trinity; incarnation; death and resurrection bring salvation; Bible and sacraments.
  • 1054: Catholic (pope, Latin) and Orthodox (patriarchs, Greek, icons) churches split; in the West the Church shaped power, learning and daily life.
  • Ethiopia was a Christian kingdom from the 4th century, with its own church and Solomonic kings; Christians also lived across Asia.

Mission 3

  • Core beliefs: tawhid, the Qur'an as God's word, Muhammad as the last prophet; the Five Pillars, Sunna and sharia shaped daily life and law.
  • Islam spread by conquest, then by merchants and Sufis; the Abbasids fragmented into Turkic sultanates; Muslim scholars transferred and advanced learning.
  • Sunni and Shi'a differ over leadership after 632; Ottoman–Safavid rivalry hardened the split; religious ideas later fueled resistance to empire.

Mission 4

  • Core beliefs: Brahman and atman; dharma, karma, samsara and moksha; many deities in Vaishnava, Shaiva and Shakta streams.
  • Society: varna (four ideal classes) and jati (many birth groups); bhakti saints offered God to all through devotion.
  • States: Vijayanagara, Rajput kingdoms, the Khmer Empire and Majapahit used temples and dharma to legitimate rule.

Mission 5

  • Core beliefs: Three Marks (anicca, dukkha, anatta), Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path and nirvana; the sangha keeps the teaching alive.
  • Branches: Theravada (arhat; South and Southeast Asia), Mahayana (bodhisattva; East Asia), Tibetan (lamas; Tibet, Mongolia).
  • Spread by Ashoka's missions, Silk Roads and sea routes; kings of Srivijaya, Sukhothai and Sri Lanka gained legitimacy by supporting the sangha.

Mission 6

  • Confucian core: ren, li (ritual), filial piety, five relationships; respect for and expected deference from women.
  • Song China chose scholar-officials by exams on the classics; Neo-Confucianism (Zhu Xi) answered Buddhism and Daoism and became exam orthodoxy.
  • These traditions spread to Korea, Heian Japan and Vietnam, each adapting them.
